paper.title: Sumo: Dynamic and Generalizable Whole-Body Loco-Manipulation

review.question: 2025-07-19 至 2026-07-19 的 loco-manipulation 研究在哪些控制、学习、数据、感知、评测和部署方向取得了可验证进展，其适用边界与未解问题是什么？

relevance.reason: Direct dynamic whole-body loco-manipulation study combining a pretrained RL controller with online sample-based planning.

sections_read.purpose: Identify dynamic manipulation of objects beyond arm payload and geometry limits.
Record MoCap, modeling and reward-engineering limits.

research_question: Can online planning steer a pretrained whole-body policy to new large-object tasks without task-specific policy retraining?
contributions: Policy-in-the-loop sample-based MPC for dynamic quadruped and simulated humanoid loco-manipulation.

method.summary: CEM plans online in the compact command space of a pretrained whole-body RL controller using parallel MuJoCo rollouts and task-specific costs.
assumptions: An adequate robot/object dynamics model is available online.
Robot and object state can be measured accurately; hardware tests use motion capture.

datasets: online model rollouts; no task-specific policy dataset
study_context.sample_or_scale: Eight Spot hardware tasks and four simulated G1 tasks; 10 trials per reported task.

evaluation.design: Simulation compares end-to-end MPC/RL and hierarchical RL; hardware case studies report success and completion time on large or heavy objects.

findings.finding: Online planning reused one low-level policy for dynamic manipulation of objects larger or heavier than the arm's nominal capacity.
findings.scope: Eight lab tasks on Spot with MoCap and manually specified task costs.

author_stated.limitation: Hardware uses MoCap; model construction still needs trial and error; task costs are manually engineered and no human/foundation-model priors are used.

reader_inferred.boundary: Test-time flexibility shifts engineering from policy retraining to modeling and cost design rather than eliminating it.
reader_inferred.basis: Each full demonstration uses a tailored task cost and a laboratory state-estimation stack.

transfer_boundary: Strong for modeled dynamic interactions with accurate state; not yet an onboard-perception or language-level autonomous system.

design_strengths: Eight quantitative real-hardware tasks with challenging object scale.
design_risks: Motion-capture state and bespoke costs simplify deployment.
critical_appraisal.baseline_fairness: The authors tune baselines in the same simulator, but reward/cost complexity differs across paradigms.
critical_appraisal.metric_validity: Binary completion and time are task-relevant; safety forces are not comprehensively measured.
critical_appraisal.reproducibility: Planning and controller interfaces are described and code is linked.
critical_appraisal.external_validity: Physical evidence is Spot-only and laboratory-based.

evidence_cards.claim: On hardware, Sumo uprighted a 15 kg tire—heavier than Spot arm's stated 11 kg lifting capacity—in 10/10 trials, averaging 9.2±4.7 seconds.
evidence_cards.relation: Supports online steering of a pretrained whole-body policy for dynamic heavy-object manipulation.
evidence_cards.summary: The hardware case study reports object mass, nominal arm capacity, success and completion time.
evidence_cards.source_context: Tire Upright:In Fig. 7 (a), the robot is tasked to upright a tire of15kg, which is heavier than the maximum lifting capacity of11kg of the Spot arm. Additionally, the rubber tire presents hard-to-model geometries and friction properties, causing a large sim-to-real gap. Using a combination of its arm, torso, and legs, Sumo enables the robot to complete the task10out of10trials with an average completion time of9.2±4.7s, Tab. II.

quantitative.comparator: 15 kg tire versus 11 kg nominal arm capacity

verification.rationale: The paragraph directly states the two masses, 10-trial result and mean completion time.
